prompt: In classical mechanics, what specifies the state of a system?

choices.text: A point (x, p) of position and momentum
A wavefunction ψ(x, t) of position and time
choices.why: That is how quantum mechanics specifies a state (Postulate I). Classical mechanics uses x and p.

choices.text: Its total energy alone
choices.why: Many different positions and momenta can share one energy. The classical state is the point (x, p).

choices.text: A probability density P(x) for its position
choices.why: Probability densities come from quantum mechanics. Classically, x and p are known exactly.

explanation: Classically, the state is a point (x, p) in the space of coordinates and momenta. It fixes everything else: any observable Q(x, p) can be worked out from it.

prompt: Why can't the state of a quantum system be specified by a point (x, p)?

choices.text: x and p can't both be known exactly at the same time
Quantum particles have no position at all
choices.why: A particle can be found at a position; the trouble is knowing its position and momentum exactly at the same time.

choices.text: Quantum particles always have zero momentum
choices.why: Quantum particles can have momentum. It just can't be known exactly together with the position.

choices.text: The point (x, p) only works for particles at rest
choices.why: The reason is the uncertainty principle: x and p can't both be known exactly.

explanation: The position-momentum uncertainty principle says x and p can't both be known exactly along a trajectory. So the classical (x, p) description fails, and quantum mechanics uses the wavefunction ψ instead.

prompt: Which experiment does the section cite as showing that an electron's position and momentum can't both be known exactly along its path?

choices.text: The diffraction of electrons
The photoelectric effect
choices.why: The photoelectric effect showed that light comes in quanta. The section points to electron diffraction.

choices.text: Blackbody radiation
choices.why: Blackbody radiation led Planck to quantized energies. The section points to electron diffraction.

choices.text: The line spectrum of hydrogen
choices.why: The hydrogen spectrum shows quantized energy levels. The section points to electron diffraction.

explanation: The diffraction of electrons shows their wave nature: it is impossible to know both the position and momentum of the electron exactly at every point along its path. That is why a new way to specify the state is needed.

prompt: What does Postulate I of quantum mechanics say?

choices.text: The state of a system is completely specified by its wavefunction ψ
The state of a system is specified by its position x and momentum p
choices.why: That is the classical picture, which fails in quantum mechanics because of the uncertainty principle.

choices.text: The wavefunction gives the exact position of the particle at all times
choices.why: ψ gives the probability of finding the particle at each position, not an exact position.

choices.text: The energy alone specifies the state of a system
choices.why: Different states can share one energy. Postulate I says ψ holds all the information.

explanation: Postulate I: the state of the system is completely specified by ψ, and all possible information about the system can be found in the wavefunction.

prompt: A wavefunction is written ψ(r, t). What are r and t?

choices.text: r is the set of the particles' spatial coordinates, and t is the time
r is the radius of the orbit, and t is the temperature
choices.why: r stands for spatial coordinates such as (x, y, z), and t for time.

choices.text: r is the rate of a reaction, and t is the time
choices.why: r is a set of positions, not a rate.

choices.text: r is the position of the first particle only, and t is the time
choices.why: For more than one particle, r includes the coordinates of every particle.

explanation: ψ(r, t) depends on the spatial coordinates and on time. For one particle r = (x_1, y_1, z_1); for n particles, r is the full set (x_1, y_1, z_1, …, x_n, y_n, z_n).

prompt: For a system of several particles, r in ψ(r, t) is the complete set of coordinates, (x_1, y_1, z_1, x_2, y_2, z_2, …). How many spatial coordinates are in r for a system of 3 particles?
explanation: Each particle has three coordinates, x, y and z, so 3 particles × 3 coordinates = 9.

prompt: Why is the wavefunction ψ sometimes called the state function?

choices.text: Because it specifies, or identifies, the state of the system
Because it tells you whether the system is a solid, liquid or gas
choices.why: "State" here means the quantum state of the system, not its state of matter.

choices.text: Because, like U or H in thermodynamics, it depends only on the start and end of a process
choices.why: The name has nothing to do with thermodynamic state functions. ψ is called this because it specifies the state.

choices.text: Because it only applies to states that never change with time
choices.why: ψ(r, t) can depend on time. The name comes from ψ identifying the state.

explanation: The state of a system is defined by its properties, and ψ determines all of them. So ψ specifies or identifies the state, and is sometimes called the state function.

prompt: In the Born interpretation, what does P(x) = ψ^*(x)ψ(x) = |ψ(x)|^2 give?

choices.text: The probability density of finding the particle at position x
The exact position of the particle
choices.why: Quantum mechanics gives probabilities, not an exact position. |ψ(x)|^2 says how likely each x is.

choices.text: The energy of the particle at position x
choices.why: |ψ(x)|^2 is a probability density, not an energy.

choices.text: The momentum of the particle at position x
choices.why: |ψ(x)|^2 tells you about where the particle is likely to be, not its momentum.

explanation: The Born interpretation says ψ^*(x)ψ(x) = |ψ(x)|^2 is the probability density P(x) that a particle in the state ψ will be found at position x. Large |ψ|^2 means the particle is likely to be found there.

prompt: At one point x_0, a wavefunction has the imaginary value ψ(x_0) = 0.6i, so its complex conjugate is ψ^*(x_0) = −0.6i. What is the probability density P(x_0) = ψ^*(x_0)ψ(x_0)?
explanation: P = (−0.6i)(0.6i) = −0.36i^2 = −0.36 × (−1) = 0.36. Multiplying by the complex conjugate always gives a real number that is zero or positive, as a probability density must be.

prompt: For the wavefunction ψ(x) = Ne^(ikx), with N a real number, what is the complex conjugate ψ^*(x)?

choices.text: Ne^(−ikx)
−Ne^(ikx)
choices.why: Taking the complex conjugate changes i to −i in the exponent; it doesn't change the sign in front.

choices.text: Ne^(ikx), the same as ψ
choices.why: ψ is complex, so its conjugate is different: i becomes −i.

choices.text: N^2e^(2ikx)
choices.why: That is ψ multiplied by itself, ψ^2, not the complex conjugate.

explanation: The complex conjugate replaces i by −i: ψ^*(x) = Ne^(−ikx). Then ψ^*ψ = N^2e^(−ikx)e^(ikx) = N^2.

prompt: A particle has the wavefunction ψ(x) = Ne^(ikx) with N = 0.3. Using P(x) = ψ^*(x)ψ(x) and e^(−ikx)e^(ikx) = 1, what is its probability density at x = 2?
explanation: P(x) = (Ne^(−ikx))(Ne^(ikx)) = N^2 = 0.3^2 = 0.09. The answer is the same at every x, and for every k.

prompt: For ψ(x) = Ne^(ikx), the probability density is P(x) = N^2, the same at every x. What does this say about the particle's position?

choices.text: It is not localized; its position is very uncertain
It is certainly at x = 0
choices.why: P(x) is the same everywhere, so x = 0 is no more likely than any other place.

choices.text: It is well localized at the crests of the wave
choices.why: The crests belong to the real part of ψ. The probability density N^2 has no peaks at all.

choices.text: It is well localized, because N^2 is a single number
choices.why: A single constant value spread over all x means the particle could be anywhere, so it is not localized.

explanation: A wavefunction like Ne^(ikx) gives the same chance of finding the particle everywhere, so its position is ill-defined and the uncertainty in position is large. This is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle in action.

prompt: A normalized wavefunction obeys the condition that the integral of ψ^*(x)ψ(x) from −∞ to ∞ equals 1. What does this mean?

choices.text: The particle is certain to be found somewhere
The particle is found at exactly x = 1
choices.why: The 1 is a total probability, not a position. It says the particle is somewhere.

choices.text: The wavefunction ψ(x) equals 1 at every point
choices.why: It is the integral of |ψ|^2 over all space that equals 1, not ψ itself at each point.

choices.text: There is a 1% chance of finding the particle
choices.why: A total probability of 1 means 100%, not 1%.

explanation: Adding up the probability density over all space must give 1: the chance of finding the particle somewhere between −∞ and +∞ is 100%.

prompt: A particle's wavefunction is normalized, so the total probability of finding it somewhere is 1. The probability of finding it inside a certain region is 0.85. What is the probability of finding it outside that region? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: The probabilities over all space add up to 1, so the probability outside the region is 1 − 0.85 = 0.15.

prompt: What makes a function f(x) square-integrable?

choices.text: The integral of f^*(x)f(x) over all x is finite
f(x) is finite at every point
choices.why: That isn't enough: cos x over (0, ∞) is finite everywhere, but the integral of cos^2 x is infinite.

choices.text: The integral of f(x) itself equals zero
choices.why: The definition is about the integral of |f(x)|^2, and it must be finite, not zero.

choices.text: f(x) is the square of another function
choices.why: "Square-integrable" means you can integrate its square and get a finite answer.

explanation: A function is square-integrable if the integral of f^*(x)f(x) = |f(x)|^2 over all x is finite. Only then can the wavefunction be normalized so that the Born interpretation applies.

prompt: A wavefunction is sharply peaked at one value of x. What does this say about the particle?

choices.text: It is well localized near the peak
It is equally likely to be found anywhere
choices.why: The probability density is peaked too, so the particle is most likely near the peak.

choices.text: It is moving very fast at the peak
choices.why: The peak describes where the particle is likely to be, not its speed.

choices.text: Its position is completely unknown
choices.why: The opposite: a sharp peak means the position is known quite well.

explanation: If ψ is sharply peaked, so is the probability density |ψ|^2. The particle is very likely near the center of the peak, and a narrow peak means a small uncertainty in its position.

prompt: A peaked wavefunction is made wider, with its peak spread over a larger range of x. What happens to the uncertainty in the particle's position?

choices.text: It increases
It decreases
choices.why: A wider peak spreads the probability over more positions, so the position is less certain.

choices.text: It doesn't change, because only the height of the peak matters
choices.why: The width of the peak is exactly what sets the uncertainty in position.

choices.text: It becomes zero
choices.why: Zero uncertainty would need an infinitely narrow peak. Widening goes the other way.

explanation: The width of the peak in |ψ|^2 measures how spread out the possible positions are. A narrow peak means a small position uncertainty; a wider one means a larger uncertainty.

prompt: Wavefunction ψ_2 has exactly the same peak shape as ψ_1, but centered at a different x. How does the particle described by ψ_2 compare?

choices.text: It is just as well localized, but at the new position
It is less well localized, because its peak has moved
choices.why: Moving the peak doesn't change its width, so the uncertainty in position is the same.

choices.text: It is not a valid wavefunction
choices.why: Shifting a valid wavefunction along x gives another valid one.

choices.text: It describes two particles, one at each peak
choices.why: ψ_2 has one peak, at a new place, and describes one particle.

explanation: All the properties of ψ_1 carry over to ψ_2: the particle is well localized, with a small uncertainty. The only difference is where the particle is likely to be found.

prompt: To satisfy the Born interpretation, which conditions must a wavefunction meet?

choices.text: It must be single-valued, continuous and finite
It must be real and positive at every point
choices.why: Wavefunctions can be complex, like Ne^(ikx), or negative. Only |ψ|^2 must be zero or positive.

choices.text: It must be periodic, like a sine wave
choices.why: e^(−x) on [0, ∞) is acceptable and is not periodic.

choices.text: It must be zero at x = 0
choices.why: That holds for some systems, such as a box with a wall at x = 0, but it is not a general rule.

explanation: A well-behaved wavefunction must be single-valued, continuous and finite. Many solutions of the Schrödinger equation fail these tests and so can't describe a physical system.

prompt: Why can't a valid wavefunction be infinite over a finite region of space?

choices.text: Its normalization integral would be infinite
Because the particle would then move infinitely fast
choices.why: The problem is with probabilities, not speed: the integral of |ψ|^2 would be infinite.

choices.text: It can, as long as it is continuous
choices.why: Being continuous doesn't help. The integral of |ψ|^2 would still be infinite.

choices.text: Because it would then not be single-valued
choices.why: It could still have one value at each point. The trouble is that the integral of |ψ|^2 becomes infinite.

explanation: If ψ were infinite over some region, the integral of |ψ|^2 would be infinite and ψ couldn't be normalized. It would mean the particle is certain to be in the infinite region and has zero probability of being anywhere else.

prompt: Why must a wavefunction be single-valued?

choices.text: Otherwise there could be two probabilities at one point
A particle can only ever be found at one place
choices.why: A particle can be found at many places, each with its own probability. The rule is one probability per point.

choices.text: ψ must take each value only once (be one-to-one)
choices.why: Single-valued means one value at each x. sin x repeats its values but is fine.

choices.text: So that it can be drawn as a smooth curve
choices.why: Smoothness is about continuity and derivatives. Single-valued means one value at each x, so one probability at each point.

explanation: If |ψ(x)|^2 had more than one value at a point, there would be several different probabilities of finding the particle there, which is absurd. So |ψ|^2, and usually ψ itself, must be single-valued.

prompt: Why must the first and second derivatives of a wavefunction exist?

choices.text: ψ must solve the Schrödinger equation, a second-order equation
So that the integral of |ψ|^2 is finite and ψ can be normalized
choices.why: Normalization needs a finite integral of |ψ|^2. The derivatives are needed for the Schrödinger equation.

choices.text: Because the probability density is the derivative of ψ
choices.why: The probability density is |ψ|^2, not a derivative.

choices.text: So that ψ has only one value at each point x
choices.why: Single-valuedness is a separate requirement. The derivatives are needed because of the Schrödinger equation.

explanation: The Schrödinger equation contains the second derivative of ψ, so it must exist. That in turn needs the first derivative to exist; otherwise ψ can't be a solution.

prompt: According to the section, when may the requirement that a wavefunction's derivatives exist be somewhat flexible in practice?

choices.text: When the potential changes rapidly with distance
When the particle is very heavy
choices.why: The section links the flexibility to the potential energy, not to the particle's mass.

choices.text: When the wavefunction is complex
choices.why: Complex wavefunctions, like Ne^(ikx), are smooth. The flexibility is tied to rapid changes in the potential.

choices.text: Never: it must hold exactly for every system
choices.why: The section says it may be somewhat flexible, particularly when the potential changes rapidly with distance.

explanation: The smoothness rule comes from the Schrödinger equation. In practice it may be somewhat flexible, particularly where the potential energy of the system shows rapid changes with distance.

prompt: Is every mathematical solution of the Schrödinger equation an acceptable wavefunction?

choices.text: No: many are rejected because they break the Born interpretation
Yes: any solution is a valid wavefunction
choices.why: Solutions that are infinite, many-valued or not square-integrable can't be normalized or read as probabilities.

choices.text: No: only solutions that are real numbers are allowed
choices.why: Complex wavefunctions, like Ne^(ikx), are allowed. The tests are being single-valued, continuous and finite.

choices.text: Yes, as long as it is finite at x = 0
choices.why: Being finite at one point is not enough. It must be well-behaved everywhere.

explanation: Many acceptable mathematical solutions of the Schrödinger equation are not acceptable physically. The Born interpretation needs ψ to be single-valued, continuous, finite and square-integrable.

prompt: In Exercise 4.1.1, cos x over (0, ∞) is single-valued and continuous. Why is it still not an acceptable wavefunction?

choices.text: It is not square-integrable
It goes to infinity as x grows
choices.why: cos x stays between −1 and 1 everywhere, so it is finite. The trouble is the integral of its square.

choices.text: It takes negative values for some x
choices.why: Negative values are fine; the probability density uses |ψ|^2, which is never negative.

choices.text: It is not continuous at x = π
choices.why: cos x is smooth and continuous everywhere.

explanation: cos x keeps oscillating forever, so the area under cos^2 x keeps growing without limit. It can't be normalized, so it fails as a wavefunction over (0, ∞).

prompt: In Exercise 4.1.1, why is e^(x) over (−∞, ∞) not an acceptable wavefunction?

choices.text: It blows up as x → ∞
It is negative when x is negative
choices.why: e^(x) is positive for every x; for negative x it just gets small.

choices.text: It has two values at some x
choices.why: e^(x) has exactly one value at each x.

choices.text: It is zero at x = 0
choices.why: e^0 = 1, not 0. The problem is the growth toward +∞.

explanation: As x → ∞, e^(x) blows up, so the integral of |e^(x)|^2 over (−∞, ∞) is infinite. The function can't be normalized.

prompt: Which of these functions from Exercise 4.1.1 is an acceptable wavefunction over the range given?

choices.text: e^(−x) over [0, ∞)
cos x over (0, ∞)
choices.why: It is finite and continuous, but the integral of cos^2 x over (0, ∞) is infinite.

choices.text: e^(x) over (−∞, ∞)
choices.why: It grows without limit as x → ∞, so it is not square-integrable.

choices.text: tan θ over [0, 2π]
choices.why: It is discontinuous, jumping to infinity within the range.

explanation: e^(−x) on [0, ∞) is single-valued, continuous and finite, and it dies away fast enough that the integral of |e^(−x)|^2 is finite (1/2). So it is square-integrable and acceptable.

prompt: Exercise 4.1.1 finds that the integral of |e^(−x)|^2 from 0 to ∞ is 1/2. To be normalized, the wavefunction Ne^(−x) needs N^2 × 1/2 = 1. What is N? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: N^2 × 1/2 = 1 gives N^2 = 2, so N = √2 = 1.414. The normalized wavefunction is √2 e^(−x) on [0, ∞).

prompt: In Exercise 4.1.1, why is tan θ over [0, 2π] not an acceptable wavefunction?

choices.text: It is discontinuous at θ = π/2 and 3π/2
It repeats itself every π
choices.why: Repeating itself is not a problem. The trouble is the breaks where tan θ goes to infinity.

choices.text: It takes negative values for some θ
choices.why: Negative values are fine for a wavefunction. The trouble is that tan θ is discontinuous.

choices.text: It has two values at every θ
choices.why: tan θ has one value wherever it is defined. It fails because it is discontinuous.

explanation: tan θ = sin θ/cos θ goes to infinity where cos θ = 0, at θ = π/2 and 3π/2. So it is neither continuous nor finite over [0, 2π].
